target_customer: Game studios and developers of interactive products that run QA testing
problem: Game and interactive software testing is slow and manual, and scripted tests break whenever the product changes. Evo.Do used reinforcement learning bots that adapt, so tests fail only on real bugs.
business_model: B2B SaaS test automation for games

founders.name: Michael Shalyt
education: MSc in quantum computing (institution not named on YC page)
previous_startups: Describes himself as a 2X co-founder and CEO of deep tech startups; names not given
founders.background_notes: Background in cyber security, algorithms, machine learning and physics per the YC founder bio.

founders.name: Nataly Bendersky Shalem
founders.background_notes: No bio on the YC page.

competitors.name: Test.ai
competitors.what: Bots that test mobile apps using AI
competitors.funding_then: 11 million dollar Series A led by Google, July 2018

technical_complexity.rationale: Deep reinforcement learning bots that learn to play arbitrary games and detect bugs was research heavy in 2018 for a two person team.

defensibility.rationale: No data or integration lock in is described, and test bot techniques were being published openly.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Later entrants such as modl.ai (founded 2018, seed 2020) pursued the same game QA bot idea; Evo.Do was reportedly inactive by September 2019.

market_need_then: Game studios spend heavily on manual QA and codeless automation was a growing topic; the company was formerly called Autoplay AI. No sourced customer demand figures were found.

brand_strength.rationale: No press, community or brand material found. The dot in the name makes it awkward to type and search, and aggregators mix it up with unrelated products.

outcome_analysis: Evo.Do was a two person Tel Aviv team building reinforcement learning QA bots for games, formerly named Autoplay AI. It joined YC in Winter 2019 with a reported 150,000 dollar seed and, per a single directory, stopped operating in September 2019. No post-mortem or press explains the cause, so it is not public and failure factors are left empty.
notes: No company website is listed and none was found; treated as dead. The 150K seed, the September 2019 shutdown and the Autoplay AI former name rest on a single directory (Startupim). A Me.sh profile still describes the CTO in the present tense. Crunchbase and the YC launch coverage give no more. Another aggregator describes a different Evo.Do (reputation management); ignored. The YC W19 blog part 4 does not feature the company. Audit note: the round is stage other because the source gives no label; amount, date and the shutdown all rest on one directory (Startupim). No source contradicts them, so data are unchanged.
